clinicalPearls: Presents as acute hypoxaemia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates developing within about six hours of transfusion
It is a form of non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, so filling pressures are normal and there is no evidence of volume overload
Often accompanied by fever, hypotension and, in severe cases, transient reduction in the circulating white-cell count
Classically attributed to donor antibodies against recipient leucocyte antigens, with a two-hit model in which patient predisposition primes the pulmonary endothelium
Plasma-rich components carry the greatest risk, and preferential use of male donor plasma has reduced incidence
Management is supportive with oxygen and respiratory support, escalating to non-invasive or invasive ventilation as required
Distinguishing it from circulatory overload is essential because diuresis is the treatment for overload but not for this injury
Report suspected cases to the blood service so implicated donors can be investigated and deferred
reference.pathophysiology: Transfusion-related acute lung injury is an acute inflammatory injury of the pulmonary capillary endothelium. In the antibody-mediated form, donor anti-leucocyte antibodies bind recipient neutrophil or human leucocyte antigens, activating neutrophils that are already sequestered in the pulmonary microvasculature. A widely used two-hit model holds that an initial insult such as sepsis or surgery primes and sequesters neutrophils, after which the transfused antibody or accumulated biological response modifiers provides the second hit. The resulting neutrophil activation damages the endothelium, increasing permeability so that protein-rich fluid floods the alveoli. Because the mechanism is inflammatory rather than hydrostatic, cardiac filling pressures remain normal.
additionalDifferentials: Acute respiratory distress syndrome from another cause
Bacterial contamination with septic reaction and shock
additionalInvestigations: Chest imaging demonstrating bilateral infiltrates without cardiomegaly or upper-lobe diversion
Arterial blood gas or pulse oximetry to quantify hypoxaemia
Natriuretic peptide levels, typically not markedly raised, to help distinguish from circulatory overload
Echocardiography or assessment of filling pressures to confirm normal cardiac function
Full blood count, which may show transient neutropenia
Testing of donor and recipient for leucocyte antibodies in conjunction with the blood service
redFlags: Rapidly worsening hypoxaemia within hours of transfusion requiring ventilatory support
Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with hypotension rather than hypertension
Failure to improve with diuresis, arguing against circulatory overload
Progressive respiratory failure despite high-flow oxygen
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve within a few days with supportive respiratory care and the pulmonary infiltrates resolve, but severe cases requiring mechanical ventilation carry appreciable mortality and it remains a leading cause of transfusion-related death.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the picture as circulatory overload and treating with diuretics that do not help
Attributing the hypoxaemia solely to the underlying illness and missing the transfusion trigger
Failing to report the reaction, so implicated donors are not investigated
Assuming a normal natriuretic peptide excludes any transfusion reaction
management: Stop the transfusion immediately and alert the transfusion service when hypoxaemia and bilateral infiltrates arise within hours of a component
Provide supportive respiratory care with supplemental oxygen escalating to non-invasive or lung-protective invasive ventilation as hypoxaemia dictates
Support hypotension with fluids and vasopressors, recognising the picture is inflammatory capillary leak with normal filling pressures
Avoid diuretic-driven fluid removal, which does not address the permeability oedema
Investigate implicated donors with the blood service for anti-leucocyte antibodies and defer them from future donation
Reduce risk through preferential use of male-donor plasma and restrictive transfusion practice
